source.title: Large Dimensional Kernel Ridge Regression: Extending to Product Kernels
source.authors: Yangfan Zhou; Yicheng Li; Yu-Qiang Cheng; Qian Lin

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper derives generalization-error convergence rates for large-dimensional product-kernel KRR and reports multiple-descent behavior as sample size varies. This is a theoretical test of the sample-size version in a different model class and setting, not a deep-network reproduction.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theoretical results on sample-size-dependent convergence rates are included. The Gaussian-kernel experiment varies dimension with n = ceil(d^1.5), so it does not isolate a sample-size effect and is not included as a row. Results cited from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The 'multiple descent' here is an oscillation in the exponent of the convergence rate of optimally regularized KRR as γ varies, where n ≍ d^γ. All derived rates are negative powers of n, so the excess risk itself never rises with more data. The paper reports no test-error peak near an interpolation threshold and no sample-size sweep at fixed d. It therefore studies a related construct, rate-exponent oscillation, rather than any version's test-error behaviour. The finding goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that large-dimensional product KRR shows minimax optimality for s≤1, saturation for s>1, periodic plateaus, and oscillation ('multiple descent') of the convergence rate with respect to n. Their statement that increasing n is 'less worthwhile' refers to a slower rate, i.e. diminishing returns. It does not mean that test error increases with more samples.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives asymptotic KRR rates for product kernels, rather than testing deep-network size or epoch sweeps or directly measuring a fixed-dimension sample-size sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported rate pattern depends on the source-condition range s and on the sample-size exponent γ; the exact-rate extrema differ across the ranges s ≤ 1, 1 < s < 2, and s ≥ 2.

fits_no_version.finding: With optimally tuned λ, the exponent of the KRR generalization-error rate in n oscillates as γ varies. The slowest rates fall at γ = p+ps (minimax, and exact for s≤1), γ = p+ps̃ (1<s<2) and γ = 3p (s≥2). Error still decreases in n; only the speed varies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In large-dimensional kernel regression with n ≍ d^γ, the optimal excess-risk rate exponent in n varies non-monotonically with γ ('multiple descent in the rate'). Plateaus mean that adding samples yields diminishing returns over some ranges, without any rise in error.

record.problems: The evidence for the sample-size claim is an asymptotic rate analysis in a joint regime n ≍ d^γ, not a direct test-error measurement while changing sample size at fixed dimension. The paper does not identify an interpolation threshold in these results.
record.rows_left_out: The Appendix C Gaussian-kernel experiment reports generalization error against dimension with n = ceil(d^1.5), rather than isolating sample-size variation. No other sample-size results relevant to V3 were reported separately.

untested.parts: All: no model-size sweep in deep networks.
Test error rising with more samples near the interpolation threshold. Only rate exponents under joint n–d scaling are derived.
Risk past an interpolation point as capacity grows. Capacity is not varied and λ is always tuned, never ridgeless.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict a peak location.
Label noise is fixed, and no error peaks or multiple peaks in the risk itself are shown. The behaviour without optimal regularization is not studied.
There is no reparameterization of complexity.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V3 limits_scope label is dropped. The paper's 'multiple descent' is defined on rate exponents under optimal regularization, not on the risk curve. The Appendix C Gaussian-kernel experiment only checks rate slopes against d at n=⌈d^1.5⌉, and was rightly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: Model-wise double descent in deep networks.

The paper reports asymptotic convergence-rate behavior under n ≍ d^γ, not a direct intervention that increases sample size while holding dimension fixed or a test-error rise specifically near an interpolation threshold.
Capacity-wise double descent across model classes and behavior past an interpolation point.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and sample count.
Dependence of peaks on label noise or variance, multiple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Whether counting complexity by an effective parameter measure turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: large dimensional product KRR
rows.size_stated: dimension d; sample size n ≍ d^γ
rows.operation_detail: Derived the exact generalization-error convergence rate as the sample-size exponent γ varies.
rows.measure: Asymptotic convergence rate of generalization error; the paper says the exact KRR curve coincides with the minimax curve for 0 < s ≤ 1.
rows.value: For the minimax rate, local maxima (slowest rate) occur at γ = p + ps and local minima (fastest rate) at γ = p + ps + s, p ∈ N+. The exact rate coincides with the minimax rate in this s range.
rows.note: This describes oscillations in the asymptotic rate while n and d vary jointly; it does not directly establish that test error rises after adding samples at fixed dimension or near an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: The row measures local extrema of the rate exponent as γ varies under n ≍ d^γ with optimal λ. A slower rate is not a rise in test error, so V3 (more samples raising error) is not measured.

rows.subject: large dimensional product KRR
rows.size_stated: dimension d; sample size n ≍ d^γ
rows.operation_detail: Derived the exact generalization-error convergence rate as the sample-size exponent γ varies.
rows.measure: Asymptotic convergence rate of generalization error.
rows.value: The exact rate has local maxima (slowest rate) at γ = p + p s̃ and local minima (fastest rate) at γ = p + p s̃ + 1, p ∈ N+, where s̃ = min{s, 2}.
rows.note: The stated extrema concern the rate under joint large-dimensional scaling, not a direct measured increase in test error from adding samples at fixed dimension.
rows.check: Same as r1: these are rate-exponent extrema for 1<s<2, not test error increasing with n. The 1<s<2 case comes from the Section 4 text.

rows.subject: large dimensional product KRR
rows.size_stated: dimension d; sample size n ≍ d^γ
rows.operation_detail: Derived the exact generalization-error convergence rate as the sample-size exponent γ varies.
rows.measure: Asymptotic convergence rate of generalization error.
rows.value: The exact rate does not change with s in this range; its local maxima (slowest rate) occur at γ = 3p and its local minima (fastest rate) at γ = 3p + 1, p ∈ N+.
rows.note: The rate oscillates with the joint-scaling exponent; the result does not directly show test error increasing after adding samples at fixed dimension.
rows.check: Same as r1: these are rate-exponent extrema for s≥2 (γ=3p and γ=3p+1), not error increasing with n.

rows.subject: minimax rate for large dimensional product kernels
rows.size_stated: dimension d; sample size n ≍ d^γ
rows.operation_detail: Derived the minimax generalization-error rate as the sample-size exponent γ varies.
rows.measure: Asymptotic minimax convergence rate of generalization error.
rows.value: The rate has local maxima (slowest rate) at γ = p + ps and local minima (fastest rate) at γ = p + ps + s, p ∈ N+.
rows.note: A minimax rate profile under joint variation of n and d is not a direct measurement of test-error increases from adding samples near an interpolation threshold.
rows.check: This is a minimax lower-bound rate profile, a property of the problem class rather than an observed behaviour of a model. It does not show error rising with samples.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
